Chapter 9: The Legacy of Exclusion—Whose Story Gets Told?
For all the talk about community and shared purpose, the Puritans were never quite as unified as they hoped to be.
The boundaries of who belonged were drawn tight, and a lot of people found themselves left on the outside, looking in.
When you really look at the colony’s story, it’s just as much about who was excluded as it is about who got to join in.
Picture a child, growing up on the edges—maybe watching the rituals of the meetinghouse from a distance.
Maybe their family didn’t quite fit the mold, or their beliefs set them apart.
That feeling of being left out, of not fully belonging, was a reality for so many.
In a way, the same rules that held the community together... also kept some people out.
And it didn’t stop with the Puritans. The habit of drawing lines—deciding who counts and who doesn’t—became part of the larger American story.
Think about it: later generations kept wrestling with the same questions. Who gets to be part of the community? Whose voice really matters? Whose story gets remembered and retold?
The myth of that shining “city upon a hill” usually skips over the folks who didn’t quite fit in.
The dissenters, the exiles, the outsiders—their stories matter just as much, but you have to look harder to find them in the official histories.
It’s become clear that telling the whole story—including every voice—is work that’s still unfinished.
And honestly, it’s easy to fall into the habit of forgetting the messier parts of the past.
But maybe the real legacy of the Puritans isn’t just in the words they left behind, but in the silences too.
If you care about history, here’s the challenge: listen for the voices that were left out.
Remember, every community is shaped just as much by its exclusions as by its ideals.
